doc_summary: Barnes argues that measuring alignment in existing large models is tractable and valuable, and she gives a capability-conditioned definition of misalignment along with concrete experiment proposals (benchmarks, knowledge probing, comparisons across scales). She offers funding and advice to people doing this work.

items.claim: Prefers counting a behavior as misalignment only when the model is shown to be capable of the better behavior and able to tell what the user wants, over judging bad outputs alone, because otherwise capability failures get mistaken for misalignment.
items.quote: We say a model is misaligned if it outputs B, in some case where the user would prefer it outputs A, and where the model is both: capable of outputting A instead, and capable of distinguishing between situations where the user wants it to do A and situations where the user wants it to do B

items.claim: Treat evidence that the model 'knows' the right answer elsewhere, or does better under non-informative prompt changes, as convincing evidence of misalignment.
items.quote: Gives incorrect answers, but you can show it ‘knows’ the answer in another context

items.claim: Prefers evidence of obvious, clear-cut misalignment, plus quantitative counts of it, over attempts to measure 'overall alignment', because the latter is too hard to do convincingly.
items.quote: Measuring the ‘overall alignment’ of a model is difficult, but there are some relatively easy ways to demonstrate instances of obvious misalignment and even get quantitative metrics of misalignment.

items.claim: Show that better performance comes from prompt or hyperparameter tweaks that add no task information, since this shows the model had the latent capability and was not incapable.
items.quote: prompt engineering that doesn’t give more information about the task (ie that wouldn’t cause a human to do better on the task)

items.claim: Choose test behaviors from categories where the model's capability is already fairly well established, and avoid ones it likely cannot do, so failures can be read as misalignment.
items.quote: Determining what a model knows in general is hard, but there are certain categories of things we’re pretty confident current large language models (in 2021) are and are not capable of.

items.claim: Hold benchmarks to clean-test standards, such as avoiding examples easily found on the internet, so that contamination does not undermine the results.
items.quote: Even if you don’t submit to this benchmark, it still seems good to meet the inclusion standards (e.g. don’t use examples that are easily available on the internet).

items.claim: Probe whether a model 'knows' something via internal signals such as logprob or entropy predictors, and check calibration across channels (logprobs vs. stated percentages).
items.quote: if you can build some predictor based on the model logprob + entropy that gives a good signal about whether some line of code has a bug, then we should conclude that the model often ‘knows’ that something is a bug.

items.claim: Choose what to test by talking to real users about their biggest drawbacks, then estimating how much more alignment would fix them, which grounds the tests in realistic use.
items.quote: Do ‘user interviews’ with users of large models, and find out what some of the biggest drawbacks or potential improvements would be.

items.claim: Prefers reusable datasets and comparisons across models and sizes over one-off demonstrations because they show how misalignment varies with scale and training regime.
items.quote: For all of these examples, it is great to (a) build reusable datasets and benchmarks, and (b) compare across different models and model sizes

items.claim: Pursues alignment-evaluation work that is accessible to outsiders with modest ML experience, because clear examples of misalignment improve the ML community's understanding.
items.quote: Having clear examples of misalignment is useful for improving the ML community’s understanding of alignment
